newsitem.title: USA: Forex pros gather as market uncertainties mount.
newsitem.headline: Forex pros gather as market uncertainties mount.

text.p: Foreign exchange dealers will converge on Toronto this week for the 39th annual congress of the world forex club amid shifting global economic fundamentals and heightened uncertainty over Europe's single currency plan.

Months of volatility-laden trading have padded the profits of many currency traders, but an increasingly cloudy economic backdrop has left delegates to this year's gathering of the Association Cambiste Internationale (ACI) with more questions than answers about the year ahead.

Suddenly, after a two-year ascent against the mark and yen, the outlook for the dollar is unclear. And as the deadline for monetary union nears, political change and economic weakness in Europe is creating unusual jitters in the markets.

"You have fundamentals that are changing very rapidly," said Sandy Batten, international economist at Citibank in New York. "That has meant a lot less clear view of where markets are going over the next few months and that's behind the volatility that we've seen."
High volume and large currency fluctuations have been friendly to volatility-hungry traders during the first five months of 1997.

The dollar, which began the year at roughly 116 yen and 1.54 marks, climbed rapidly to multi-year peaks of 127.47 yen and 1.7389 marks one month ago, before succumbing to broad sales and tumbling back to lows below 112 yen and 1.67 marks in recent weeks.
"Six months ago the volumes and volatilities were down," said David DeRosa, managing partner at Quadrangle Investments, a hedge fund based in Greenwich, Connecticut.
"But the last three to six months have been very good to the industry. You have had all these violent movements, lots of choppy periods and considerable flows."
Recent developments have produced an increasingly murky outlook, however.

U.S. economic growth, which appeared so robust when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in late March, now appears to be slowing. And In Japan, the early stages of a recovery appear underway and talk of a hike in official rates has boosted the yen.
Recent elections in Britain have brought a more Europe-friendly government to power, while this weekend's French vote could have the opposite effect there.

"There is this cloud of EMU hanging over us," said Kevin Lawrie, head of global foreign exchange at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "There is a lot of uncertainty as to the future of the market, what it will look like, who will be in, and who will be out."

The implications of EMU for the foreign exchange industry include dwindling intra-European trades -- the bread and butter of many European banks. Consolidation is likely to accelerate, producing fewer, bigger players, dealers said.
Banks are likely to focus increasingly on emerging markets -- in Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America -- where hefty interest rate spreads and greater risks lurk.

"I imagine there are hundreds of traders and dozens of dealing rooms that will have to come up with something else to trade," said Ezra Zask, president of Barrington Capital Management, an emerging markets fixed income and currency hedge fund based in Massachusetts.
"It's a natural for German banks to start looking at Eastern Europe because they're already doing trades and investments with these countries."
Speakers at this year's gathering are scheduled to speak about opportunities in China, South Africa and Chile, among other countries.
Consolidation and technological advances -- such as electronic broking -- have already taken their toll on trading desks.
This is expected to continue and will be another hot topic of discussion at this week's conference, dealers said.

"We've had bank to bank mergers and now we're starting to see bank to brokerage mergers, bank to investment bank mergers, bank to fund manager mergers," said Mellon's Lawrie. "That just seems to be the way the industry is moving."
